newsitem.title: ITALY: Arafat, in Italy, says Netanyahu meeting was good.
newsitem.headline: Arafat, in Italy, says Netanyahu meeting was good.

text.p: Palestian President Yasser Arafat said on Thursday that his landmark meeting with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was "good" and that he believed the implementation of Middle East peace would continue.
The two men met for the first time on Wednesday for a brief summit on the Israel-Gaza border to relaunch stalled talks on extending Palestinian self-rule in the West Bank and Gaza.

Though they did not solve major problems, the meeting and a reserved handshake were seen as vital symbols of both sides' commitment to the Oslo agreement signed with the PLO by the Labour government which right-winger Netanyahu toppled in May.
"It was a good meeting but the most important thing is that we will continue the implementation of what we have begun," Arafat said in Rome, where he is on a one-day visit.

Arafat spoke to reporters in Rome after he and the Vatican's top diplomats, Cardinal Angelo Sodano and Archbishop Jean-Louis Tauran, discussed the thorny question of the status of Jerusalem and difficulties in the Middle East peace process.
The Vatican did not say why Arafat did not meet Pope John Paul, who is at his summer palace south of Rome ahead of a weekend trip to Hungary. Arafat and the Pope have met several times in the past.

A Vatican statement said Arafat and Sodano had cordial talks, which covered the "existing difficulties" in peace negotiations between Israel and the Palestinian Authority and "the delicate problem" of Jerusalem.
The Vatican wants international guarantees protecting Jerusalem as a city sacred to Moslems, Christians and Jews. Israel says the city's holy places are open to all believers.
Israel declared Jerusalem its "united and eternal" capital in 1980, 13 years after its forces captured the city's Arab eastern sector from Jordan in the Six-Day War.
Palestinians view East Jerusalem as the capital of a future state. Its fate is up for negotiation at final peace talks.
Most states, including the Vatican, have not recognised Jerusalem as the Jewish state's capital and keep their embassies elsewhere, mostly in Tel Aviv and its suburbs.

One highlight of Arafat's visit is expected to be a private meeting with Rome community leaders, hosted by mayor Francesco Rutelli at city hall. Rutelli has invited several leading members of Italy's Jewish community to attend.

It is believed to be the first time Arafat will meet members of the Italian Jewish community, which still vividly remembers a 1982 Palestinian guerrilla attack on Rome's synagogue that killed a two year-old boy.

The union of young Italian Jews asked Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini, who was due to meet Arafat on Thursday afternoon, to press him to hand over a Palestinian who was convicted in his absence in 1988 to life imprisonment for the synagogue attack.
Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy also met Dini in Rome on Thursday. Diplomats said Levy and Arafat were not expected to meet.
Arafat was due to fly north later on Thursday for an international business forum at the Italian resort of Cernobbio.

Israel's former prime minister Shimon Peres, one of the architects of the Oslo peace accord and the man Netanyahu defeated in the May election, is also scheduled to take part in the Cernobbio gathering, which begins on Friday.
